layer0_index.name: Section Three: After the War
layer0_index.description: Post-war era: Doc Adams, ritual development, national expansion, and the Ashe statue.
layer0_index.one_sentence_summary: Section Three: After the War: Post-war era: Doc Adams, ritual development, national expansion, and the Ashe statue. (13 subsections)

layer1_summary.paragraph: The post-war era marked a critical rebirth for Iron Arrow, as the society transitioned from a nearly forgotten relic into a formalized, thriving institution at the University of Miami. The arrival of Dr. Thurston Adams in 1947, his discovery of the society's bronze plaque amid campus debris, and his subsequent partnership with returning veterans and university leadership set the stage for decades of growth, ritual refinement, and eventually a push toward national recognition.
bullets: Dr. Thurston Adams arrived at the University of Miami in September 1947 and discovered a discarded Iron Arrow bronze plaque, an act that directly catalyzed the society's post-war revival.

Returning student veteran Al Adler reconnected with Adams after hearing about the plaque, passionately described Iron Arrow's pre-war significance, and committed to rebuilding the organization alongside other returning members.

Doc Adams and Dr. Ashe collaborated to develop and formalize the tapping ritual and ceremonial traditions that would define Iron Arrow's identity for generations, lending the society its distinctive solemn and Native American-inspired character.

The society's visibility and prestige grew through public events such as Homecoming parades, drum vigils, and tapping ceremonies, with figures like Chief C. Rhea Warren leading public inductions that became a celebrated campus tradition.

A pivotal moment in the society's broader recognition came when Iron Arrow pursued and ultimately achieved a national profile, while the commissioning of the Ashe statue served as a permanent tribute to one of the organization's most foundational leaders.

layer2_details.text:
DOC ADAMS ARRIVES

- Thurston Adams reported to the University of Miami on September 1, 1947
- At the time of his arrival, part of UM was still at old "North Campus"
- "Main Campus" had only one completed, permanent building: Memorial Classroom
- Merrick Building was an old "skeleton" covered with vegetation — remains of what UM had started in 1926 or 1928
- Remainder of campus was strewn with wood structures ("shacks") obtained from the Armed Services
- Adams found a bronze, "shield-shaped" plaque among debris near a shack used as "The Slop Shop," slated to be hauled away
- The plaque bore the inscription "IRON ARROW" and names
- Adams took the plaque to Curtis Weaver's office in the maintenance department (under Memorial Classroom)
- Weaver was not in; Adams left it with instructions for Weaver to be shown the plaque
- Weaver later brought it to Adams's office (second floor of old wooden building across from the Riviera Golf Course)
- Weaver said the plaque had been brought down from North Campus but wasn't sure "it amounted to anything now, after the War"
- Adams kept the plaque behind his desk, convinced it was "valuable and still important, even after the four years of W.W. II"
- Student veteran Al Adler, who had been at UM before the war, walked into Adams's office after hearing about the plaque
- Adler identified the plaque and visibly reacted with emotion — Adams noted "His eyes really beamed" and "he really 'cuddled' it"
- Adler told Adams that Iron Arrow before the war was "the finest, highest, most wonderful thing in the world"
- Adler said he and several other old members were back and intended to "get it going again"
- Adams offered to assist if needed
- Source: Thurston Adams, letter to the author, July 1, 1974

DOC'S TAPPING AND THE RITUAL

- Thurston Adams was tapped on January 17, 1950, at the first semester's honors assembly in the Lecture Hall
- Adams was told he was the first honorary Iron Arrow member ever tapped after being on campus for only three years
- Adams had believed Iron Arrow "took only students, and, quite rarely some faculty or administration member who had been at the UM since its beginning"
- During the three years before his tapping (1947–1950), Adams assisted members by: providing meeting places, helping with engraving on the old plaque, and opening the old Student Club at night for initiations
- After initiation, Adams asked where the ritual was kept — there was none; only scattered notes jotted by older members prior to selection and tapping
- Notes used for Adams's own selection, tapping, and initiation were divided among members; the greatest portion was believed to be in the automobile trunk of Art Grace
- Adams collected every scrap of paper from Grace and created a private, locked file for Iron Arrow in his office
- Subsequently, bits of information were gathered from pre-WWII graduated members, faculty members, etc.
- Adams's office covered the cost of having the ritual printed on parchment and bound; kept locked in his safe, withdrawn only for official purposes
- The old leather-bound ritual was the result of work by David McDonald, Clive Shrader, Carl Fromhagen, Frazier Payton, and Carl Cohen
- The ritual book reads: "Written and compiled in 1950 by Carl Fromhagen, Jr., assisted by Clive Shrader, Frazier Payton, and Carl Cohen"
- Carl Fromhagen's father owned a printing press and produced it at cost
- The original ritual book was later damaged by repeated handling during initiations and was once misplaced for several weeks by a faculty Iron Arrow member who left it in his desk drawer after an initiation
- The tribe approved Adams having a copy made; Carl Fromhagen's father likely produced the copy as well
- Source: Thurston Adams, letter to the author, July 1, 1974

DOC AND DR. ASHE

- Upon becoming a member, Adams found Iron Arrow was in poor financial condition: very few old, dirty jackets; no place to display the plaque; no money whatsoever
- Adams went to Dr. Ashe and requested appropriation of funds for the tribe
- Adams cited his own expenditures: plaque engraving, printing of the first recorded ritual
- Dr. Ashe acknowledged money was scarce: "Money was the shortest thing we had"
- Ashe asked if Adams could continue to help the tribe from his own account
- Adams agreed, but asked that if he ran a little over his budget, Ashe would "sweeten" it slightly
- Ashe's response (paraphrased by Adams, not confirmed verbatim): "You know, that's the way we'll handle it. That group (or that tribe) is dear to my heart!"
- This arrangement — Adams covering costs with occasional supplementation from Ashe — continued for "quite a few years"
- Immediately after this conversation, Iron Arrow acquired "a few" new jackets to supplement the small number of old, dry-cleaned ones
- No member owned a jacket personally — all jackets belonged to the tribe
- Source: Thurston Adams, letter to the author, July 1, 1974 (footnote 79: Ibid.)

THE TRADITION PROSPERS

- The period from 1947 to 1951 is identified as the first major burst of activity in consolidating Iron Arrow since its founding year
- Three major eruptions of activity identified in Iron Arrow's history: (1) at founding, (2) early post-war period 1947–1951, (3) from 1968 to the present
- Author attributes these bursts to an "organization's instinct of self-preservation" rather than solely to individual personalities
- In early spring 1948, two important events occurred: Clive Shrader was tapped into Iron Arrow, and Marvin Green was elected Chief
- Shrader recalled no large initiation: "...just a small dinner party at the Dixie Belle Restaurant on South Dixie Highway (since burned down)"
- Members' stated goal: "We determined to rejuvenate the society to the active group which Dr. Ashe had originally envisioned, and a position which the society had held prior to World War II"
- Numerous meetings were held over the following two years
- The tribe sent out calls for help to members from years gone by; the response was described as "overwhelming"
